A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ADAPT research work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables and figures, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v6 reports original classification experiments, efficiency measurements, ablations and distribution analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v8 retains those original results and adds repeated-stream stability measurements, controlled comparisons, pruning experiments and noisy long-tailed evaluation.

M1.justification: The Gaussian classifier, knowledge-bank selection, regularized objectives and online/transductive inference procedures remain unchanged. Explicit pruning is tested as an ablation; v8 expressly retains the original bank design after observing worse results.

E1.justification: The existing natural-shift, corruption, fine-grained and few-shot coverage is retained. v8 adds a long-tailed ImageNet-1K population with deliberately corrupted early predictions (Table 23), introducing an imbalance-and-noise scenario within the existing classification domain.

E2.justification: Table 18 adds TDA to the six-prompt comparison that previously reported ADAPT alone in Table 7. Table 19 adds AWT comparisons on the fine-grained datasets and an augmentation-free AWT* variant. T3A and DPCore appear only in a conceptual comparison, not newly reported performance evaluations.

E3.justification: v8 substantially extends the evaluation design with matched-prompt comparisons, augmentation removal for AWT, periodic per-class pruning, and power-law sampling with early prediction corruption. Pruning occurs every 1,000 samples at four ratios; the noise experiment corrupts 30% of high-confidence predictions during the first 30% of adaptation. Retained benchmark settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test prompt-related confounding, AWT's augmentation dependence, the effect of explicit bank pruning, and robustness to early memory contamination in long-tailed data. A randomized-stream stability study is also added. These substantially extend the existing component, covariance, input-order, corruption-severity and sample-scarcity analyses.

E5.justification: New Section B.1 and Table 13 report accuracy means and standard deviations over 10 random online-stream permutations across all three tasks. v6 lacks corresponding accuracy-variability reporting, although its projection-based normality tests already use repetitions and p-values. This establishes newly reported repetition and uncertainty, not an increase from a specified earlier run count.

E6.justification: Retained result entries are unchanged, but substantial new comparative and robustness findings are reported. Table 18 shows online ADAPT at 66.53% versus TDA at 65.92% with GPT prompts on Task 1. Table 22 shows ImageNet-A accuracy falling from 63.32% to 50.69% with 10% pruning. Table 23 reports 64.27% versus CLIP's 63.25% under the new noisy long-tailed setting. These are added experimental contrasts, not improvements over v6 under unchanged conditions.

T1.justification: The Gaussian, shared-covariance and uniform-prior assumptions, mathematical objectives, and GDA and adaptation derivations remain unchanged, including Appendix A's equations and proofs. The added protocol discussion and imbalance experiments introduce no revised mathematical model.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims: source-free, backpropagation-free Gaussian adaptation with closed-form inference, online/transductive applicability, and robust, scalable performance. The appendix additions provide further support without redefining those core contributions.

C2.justification: v8 adds interpretations connecting matched-prompt gains to distribution modeling, pruning losses to discarded informative samples, and resilience to accumulating better statistics. It explicitly acknowledges vulnerability of extremely few-shot tail classes. Existing Gaussian-model limitations remain. Its new reference to a main-paper prior-removal analysis has no clearly identifiable counterpart in the retained ablations.

D1.justification: v8 documents the new pruning cadence and ratios, long-tailed class/image counts, and prediction-corruption schedule. These improve documentation of the added experiments. Hardware, core hyperparameters, bank capacities and the project-access link remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v8 adds T3A and DPCore references and compares their mechanisms and protocol assumptions with ADAPT and DynaPrompt in Table 12. It also expands discussion of distinctions from TDA and AWT. The main related-work narrative and central research positioning are retained.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section structure remain unchanged. v8 inserts a stability subsection, expands appendix discussions, updates the contents and cross-references, and makes small notation and grammar clarifications. Existing appendix subsections are principally renumbered.

P2.justification: The appendix gains a protocol-comparison matrix, a multi-task mean/standard-deviation table, prompt and augmentation comparison tables, and pruning and noisy-tail tables (Tables 12, 13, 18, 19, 22 and 23). This substantially expands the displayed evidence. All six figures are unchanged, while existing tables are retained and renumbered or reflowed.

improvement.justification: v8 makes the empirical support more assessable through repeated-stream uncertainty reporting, matched-prompt and augmentation controls, and tests exposing pruning sensitivity and tail-class vulnerability. These strengthen evaluation of stability and comparative benefits. The gain is tempered by an unsupported reference to a prior-removal analysis and a progressive self-correction interpretation supported only by final accuracies. Overall, the additions provide a useful but limited quality improvement.
